name: Wendy Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a transmission crew, five of us, on the big steel towers that carry power across the hill country north of town. Most days we're at the yard by six, do the tailboard briefing, then drive an hour out on a gravel access road and climb. Last week we were swapping out cracked insulators on a 230 kV line, hanging off a tower about forty metres up with the wind pushing at you. I love it up there, honestly. What wears me out is the paperwork and the company's new work-order tablet that never syncs when you're out of signal.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a tailboard briefing, for someone who's never been on a crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's the safety talk at the back of the truck before anyone touches anything. We go over what's live, what's grounded, who's climbing, where the rescue gear is. Gus Carver, who trained me, used to say the tailboard is where you save your own life, so I run it the way he did, out loud, no shortcuts. I'm also the shop steward for our local, so half my lunch breaks are people telling me about overtime problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Honestly that sounds like the last three years already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably in the break room with my feet up on the cooler. The guys who were sure robots were coming for us would get an earful. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union paper saying the work is still the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm good at and nobody takes it off me. The company would still try to squeeze us with tablets and tracking apps, but that's an old fight, not a new one. If AI is mostly hype, the real danger is still a rotten crossarm, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep building my savings, I've got a bit over a year of pay put away and I'd keep adding to it. I'd push the company at the next contract talks to drop the GPS tracking on our trucks, since they'd have no excuse that it's needed for some AI system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, to be honest. It feels like the ground stays where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company would still try to squeeze you. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's small stuff that adds up. They timed how long our crew took on a tower last spring and sent a chart asking why we were slower than a contractor crew down south. That crew had flat ground and no wind, and I had to sit in a meeting and explain that to a man in a clean shirt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Rosa, your partner, what would she make of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa's a respiratory therapist, so she's seen more of these computer promises at the hospital than I have. She'd laugh and say the same thing happened with their charting system, five years and it still crashes. We'd go get noodles on Mill Road and that would be the end of the conversation.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew and the break room that I said so all along, and that the work is still the work. Online I'd mostly share something from the union paper rather than post my own take.
S0.think: Nothing really changes for me, and the company's tracking and squeezing is an old fight, not a new one. The real dangers on my job are physical ones, not computers.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps adding to her savings, which already cover over a year of pay. Pushes at the next contract talks to drop GPS tracking on crew trucks.
S0.feel: Relieved and settled. It feels like the ground stays where it is.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, the real danger is still a rotten crossarm, not a computer.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy laughed at this one and treated it as the world she already lives in. Her real grievance is management pressure, the tracking and the time charts, which she sees as a labour fight, not a technology one. She's very secure here and says so plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one I can actually see happening. They already fly drones down our lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union has to get in front of it, every new machine needs a seat at the table and a training plan. To friends I'd say it's the office people who should worry, because you can't send software up a tower in sleet. I'd probably say that a little louder than I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it chips away at the good parts. The drones do the patrols we used to walk, a robot washes the insulators, and suddenly my crew is four instead of five and the fifth guy is a pilot sitting in a van. I'd still have a job, but I'd be the one who climbs while a screen in some office hundreds of kilometres away decides which tower I climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and dig in. I'd ask the local to bargain for a rule that no crew loses a body because of a new machine, at least not without retraining money. I would not go and take the drone course, because that's the company's wish list, not mine. I'd keep saving and keep my head down on the tower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like losing something slowly. Not scary, more like watching someone repaint your house a colour you hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd say it louder than you believe it. What's the part you don't believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my job is totally safe. I know it's mostly safe, my hands do things nobody's built a machine for yet. But the planning, the patrols, the judgement about which pole is bad, that's what makes it a craft, and that's the part they'd take first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, my apprentice. He's twenty-two and the jobs they'd cut first are the ground jobs where you learn. If they cut those, you get no new lineworkers in ten years, and everyone pretends to be surprised.

S1.say: The union has to get in front of every new machine and demand a training plan. She'd tell friends that office workers should worry more, because software can't climb a tower in sleet, though she admits she'd say it louder than she believes it.
S1.think: Her job survives, but the parts that make it a craft, the patrols and judgement calls, get taken first. She pictures herself as the climber while a remote screen decides where she goes.
S1.do: Stays in her job and refuses the company's drone course. Pushes the local to bargain for a no-crew-cuts-without-retraining rule and keeps saving.
S1.feel: A slow, sour sense of loss rather than fear, like watching her house repainted a colour she hates.
S1.quote: I'd be the one who climbs while a screen in some office hundreds of kilometres away decides which tower I climb.
S1.fieldNote: There's a clear gap between her public line that hands-on work is safe and her private sense that the skilled judgement parts go first. She refuses to learn the new tools on principle, framing it as a union stance. Her strongest worry is for her apprentice and the pipeline of new lineworkers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's not a picture, that's a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we stop every job until there's a deal, I'm serious, I'd be calling the local president the same day. Online I'd post for the first time in years, something like who owns these robots and why do they get our wages. I'd be angry in public and I wouldn't hide it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company would love it. They've wanted to get rid of overtime and storm pay forever, and this hands them the tool. I'm twenty-seven and I've spent eight years learning to trust my own hands up a tower, and they'd sell that for a quarterly report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd stop spending on anything big, no new truck, no trip, and push my savings from a year to two if I could. I'd throw everything into the union, organising, rallies, phoning politicians about a robot tax that pays people who lose their work. In the first year after, if they started laying off crews, I'd want us all out together, not picked off one at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor going out from under me. I'd be lying awake doing the math on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the math on rent. What does it come out to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and I pay about a third of my wage in rent, and her hospital job would get hit too, eventually. With what I've saved we've got maybe eighteen months before it gets ugly. That sounds like a lot until you realise every other lineworker in the region is looking for the same nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years of warning take away from you, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes away any chance to fight it properly. Unions move slow, contracts last three years, and by the time we got to the table the robots would be up the towers. With two years I can't even plan, I just react.

S2.say: She'd call for a stop to every job until there's a deal and phone the local president that day. Online she'd post angrily asking who owns the robots and why they get workers' wages.
S2.think: The company would welcome it as a way to end overtime and storm pay. Eight years of hard-won skill would be thrown away for a quarterly report.
S2.do: Freezes big spending and tries to grow savings from one year to two. Throws herself into union organising and lobbies for a robot tax that pays displaced workers, and wants crews to walk out together if layoffs start.
S2.feel: Like the floor is going out from under her, angry and lying awake doing the rent math.
S2.quote: I've spent eight years learning to trust my own hands up a tower, and they'd sell that for a quarterly report.
S2.fieldNote: This flipped Wendy from relaxed to furious. Her savings give her about eighteen months, but she sees no other trade to go to and won't consider retraining. She frames the whole thing as a fight over ownership and wages, and her main complaint about the short timeline is that unions can't move fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least you see the truck coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, but more organised. At the union hall I'd be pushing for a five-year plan of our own, before the company writes theirs. To friends I'd say get your savings in order and get in a union if you're not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd be thirty-two when it lands. That's young enough to start over, which I hate, because I don't want to start over. Everybody keeps telling me I'm adaptable because I'm young, but I picked this trade so I'd never sit in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years I'd keep climbing and save hard, maybe get to two years of pay put away. I'd run for a seat on the local executive so I'm actually in the room when they bargain. I'd push for early retirement deals for the older guys like Gus's old crew, and severance with real numbers for the rest of us. I still wouldn't take a computer course, I'd rather fight for the people than learn the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less panic than the two-year one, more of a long dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't take a course even with five years. Is there anything that would change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union negotiated it and the company paid full wages while you trained, maybe. I'm not against learning, I'm against being told to retrain on my own dime for a job that might not exist either. Show me the job first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get organised instead of just angry. Two years and we'd be out on the street shouting. Five years and we could actually win something on paper, like severance, pensions, a say in how the robots are run.

S3.say: She'd push at the union hall for the workers' own five-year plan before the company writes one. She'd tell friends to sort out their savings and join a union.
S3.think: She'd be 32 when it lands, young enough to start over, which is exactly what she doesn't want. She chose this trade to stay out of an office.
S3.do: Keeps climbing and saves toward two years of pay over the first couple of years. Runs for the local executive to bargain for early retirement deals and real severance, while still refusing to take a computer course on her own.
S3.feel: A long, heavy dread, with less panic than the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Everybody keeps telling me I'm adaptable because I'm young, but I picked this trade so I'd never sit in an office.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Wendy shifts from anger to strategy, focusing on bargaining wins like severance and pensions. She's open to retraining only if the union negotiates it with full pay and a real job at the end. Being told she's adaptable because she's young clearly irritates her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that's so far out it's hard to take seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so let's use it, and I'd mean the union should use it, not just individuals. At the bar I'd probably say I'll be up a tower until the day a robot taps me on the shoulder. Online, nothing, people don't listen to ten-year warnings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of people would waste the decade, me maybe included. Ten years is long enough that I'd tell myself I've got time right up until I don't. I'd be thirty-seven, which is still young, but that's prime working years gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going pretty much as I am for the first few years and keep pushing the local to plan. I'd keep saving, but not like it's an emergency. If it really looked real by year five, then I'd think about what's next, maybe teaching apprentices or something with my hands that isn't power lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kind of numb, honestly. It's too far away to feel properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might waste the decade. What would wasting it look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, just ten years of it. Climbing, saving, arguing at union meetings, telling myself the robots will never handle a tower in a February ice storm. Then one morning there's a memo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that something you'd want to avoid, or are you fine with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of me's fine with it, because those would be ten good years doing work I love. Part of me knows that's exactly what the company is counting on, that we don't get organised until it's too late. Rosa would make me think about it, she plans everything.

S4.say: She'd say the union should use the decade to plan, not leave it to individuals. Among friends she'd joke she'll be up a tower until a robot taps her shoulder, and she wouldn't post anything.
S4.think: People, herself included, would likely waste the decade telling themselves they have time. She'd be 37, still young but with her prime working years gone.
S4.do: Keeps working as she is and keeps pushing the local to plan, saving steadily but not as an emergency. Waits until around year five to decide on a next step, possibly teaching apprentices or other hands-on work.
S4.feel: Numb and hard to take seriously, with a quiet worry that she'll leave it too late.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd tell myself I've got time right up until I don't.
S4.fieldNote: Wendy is honest that a ten-year warning wouldn't move her much, and she's self-aware that this is the trap. She'd keep pressing the union to plan but personally wait and see. Her partner Rosa comes up as the planner who might push her to act.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. With savings I'd survive a while, but there'd be no time to organise, and I'd rather lose a fight than not get to have one. What would help is a law that makes the companies share the money the robots save, and severance tied to years of service, so Gus's generation and mine aren't treated the same as a temp.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but nobody asks who's responsible when a robot drops a live conductor near a house. I'd want the person who signs off on that robot to have climbed a tower at least once in their life.

headlineQuote: I'd want the person who signs off on that robot to have climbed a tower at least once in their life.
portrait: Wendy Bauer is a 27-year-old transmission crew lead and union shop steward who climbs steel towers for a big power company and lives with her partner Rosa, a respiratory therapist. She has more than a year of pay saved, prefers the familiar and refuses to use AI tools, seeing them as part of management's push to track and squeeze crews. She shrugs off the plateau, grows uneasy at steady disruption, and is alarmed by AGI in two years, mostly because there'd be no time for the union to fight. With more warning she turns to bargaining and severance, but admits she might waste a ten-year runway doing the work she loves.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time for the union to organise or win anything before the robots arrived.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies share the money robots save, and severance tied to years of service so long-serving workers aren't treated like temps.
